walters:W.185.65V.summary: Against a chequered ground of gold, blue and red, Christ in a purple robe and crown of thorns stoops under a great wooden cross as he walks to the left. Soldiers in short tunics press round him, while the Virgin and John follow in grief at the back. The full-page miniature, framed by delicate sprays of gold ivy, opens a section of the prayers on Christ's Passion.
facts: The book is named after Franchoise de Doffinnes, who owned it in the late 16th century; her family's later history is recorded on its final folios.

Its calendar follows the Use of Utrecht and its Hours of the Virgin largely the Use of the Windesheim Congregation, pointing to a Dutch origin; it contains both Latin and Dutch texts and twelve full-page miniatures by the Master of Walters 185.
walters:W.185.65V.notes: Museum date (1400–1425) applies to the whole Book of Hours; the date in our data (8th century) was an import error.

wga:zgothic/mosaics/8/4byzant1.summary: Against a field of gold, Christ sits enthroned in a deep blue robe, blessing with his right hand and holding a jewelled Gospel book in his left, the letters IC XC beside his head. Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos offers a purse to him and Empress Zoe holds a scroll recording her gifts to the church. This imperial donor panel set the rulers of Byzantium in the very presence of Christ, before whom even an emperor approaches as a suppliant giver.
facts: The heads of all three figures were scraped off and replaced; the earlier panel may have shown Zoe's first husband Romanos III or her second husband Michael IV.
The mosaic is on the east wall of the southern gallery of Hagia Sophia.
Constantine IX Monomachos, Zoe's third husband, reigned from 1042 to 1055.
wga:zgothic/mosaics/8/4byzant1.notes: WGA gives 1034–42 and lists the period as 1101–1150, which is wrong. Wikipedia dates the mosaic only to the 11th century; the present heads date from after Constantine IX's accession in 1042.
